growth cone collapse can be subdivided into two distinct modes: fold collapse, which leads to a halt in neurite extension and a temporary reorganization of the cytoskeleton, and full collapse, which leads into neurite retraction.

growth cones of NG108-15 cells can collapse by two distinct modes of retraction, namely by full retraction of the neurite or by folding and lateral movement of filopodial actin bundles that limit microtubular extension.
we could identify a new intermediate form of growth cone collapse that is characterized by the lateral movement and folding up of filopodia.

a detailed analysis of neurite retraction and growth cone collapse in a model system.
the dynamics of growth cones in response to environmental changes and the underlying mechanisms of neurite retraction and collapse.
the identification and analysis of growth cone collapse mechanisms, and the elucidation of their underlying dynamics and functional significance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

growth cones can be collapsed by a multitude of mechanisms and that the final outcome of collapse is dependent upon the nature and strength of the guidance cue, the duration of exposure and the type of growth cone.
the two modes of growth cone retraction (fold collapse and retraction) are not mutually exclusive and that both can be observed in one and the same growth cone.
growth cones can be collapsed in two different ways, either by a rapid actin-based retraction mechanism, or by a slower, microtubule-dependent fold collapse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
growth cone collapse is a highly regulated and reversible process, which can be triggered by a multitude of different cues and which can lead to a variety of distinct outcomes.
the growth cone is able to react to a variety of stimuli by different mechanisms of collapse and retraction, which are not mutually exclusive.
the two modes of growth cone retraction represent a continuum of growth cone collapse mechanisms that are regulated by the balance of the microtubule cytoskeleton, actin turnover and actin bundling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
growth cones can react to guidance cues in a highly dynamic fashion, and that they are able to control their own extension rate by a complex interplay of cytoskeletal dynamics.
growth cone collapse can be a reversible process and does not necessarily result in neurite retraction.
collapse and retraction are two distinct processes, which can be separated by the mode of filamentous actin dynamics and the extent of microtubule involvement.
